cases.holding: The SJC held that the "reasonable cause" standard governs only the initial ex parte emergency hearing under G. L. c. 119, § 24, and that a decision to maintain removal at the seventy-two hour hearing must instead be supported by a fair preponderance of the evidence; the District Court's use of the lower standard was improper and a new hearing was ordered.
cases.quote: A new seventy-two hour hearing determination must be made in the District Court, based on a “fair preponderance of the evidence.”

relevance.INP-01: The case begins with G. L. c. 119, § 51A reports of neglect, and the court treats those reports as the statutory trigger for the department's investigation and subsequent emergency petition.
relevance.INP-02: The court describes how successive § 51A reports from different sources accumulated into the factual basis for emergency intervention.
relevance.INP-06: The court explains that "reasonable cause to believe" in the § 51A reporting context means "known or suspected instances of child abuse and neglect," a deliberately low threshold for intake.
relevance.INP-10: Robert traces the escalation from § 51A report, to investigation, to § 24 petition, and fixes the proof standard at each stage.
relevance.INP-12: This is the controlling Massachusetts authority on the burden the Commonwealth must carry to keep a child in protective custody after an emergency taking.
relevance.DEC-04: Robert supplies the constitutional floor for the emergency-removal decision: reasonable cause at the ex parte stage, fair preponderance within seventy-two hours.
relevance.ACT-03: A foster placement made on emergency authority cannot be continued past the seventy-two hour hearing unless the department proves the statutory grounds by a fair preponderance.

cases.holding: The SJC held that parents in a care and protection proceeding are entitled to the effective assistance of appointed counsel, measured by the criminal-law Saferian standard, but affirmed because the department proved unfitness by clear and convincing evidence and the ineffectiveness claim was not properly raised below.
cases.quote: Accordingly, we conclude that parents are entitled to the effective assistance of counsel pursuant to G. L. c. 119, § 29.

relevance.INP-04: The court describes the G. L. c. 119, § 23 court-appointed investigator's report as the evidentiary spine of the adjudication, showing how judicially ordered investigation feeds the case.
relevance.DEC-05: Once a petition is filed, appointed counsel attaches under § 29 and the department carries the clear-and-convincing burden on unfitness.
relevance.OUT-05: A parent who shows constitutionally ineffective counsel may obtain relief from the resulting custody judgment, but ordinarily must raise the claim below rather than for the first time on appeal.
relevance.FAIL-01: Stephen is the source of the Massachusetts ineffective-assistance standard used to attack agency-obtained custody and termination judgments.

cases.holding: The SJC held that on a petition for review and redetermination under G. L. c. 119, § 26, the moving party bears only an initial burden of producing credible evidence of changed circumstances, after which the department must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the child is still in need of care and protection; the burden may never be shifted to the parent.
cases.quote: we conclude that in a petition for review and redetermination, the department bears the ultimate burden to prove that the child is still in need of care and protection

relevance.DEC-05: Erin holds that the department, not the parent, always carries the burden in a c. 119 proceeding, at the initial adjudication and on every later review.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification is obtained through the § 26 review and redetermination mechanism, and Erin allocates the burdens that govern that hearing.
relevance.OUT-04: The appeal was dismissed as moot when Erin turned eighteen, illustrating that Juvenile Court care and protection jurisdiction in Massachusetts terminates at the child's eighteenth birthday.
relevance.OUT-05: A child is discharged from the department's custody when the department can no longer carry its clear-and-convincing burden that the child remains in need of care and protection.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Juvenile Court judge's placement of the burden on the mother was error, and Erin is the authority for reversing a redetermination decision on that ground.

cases.holding: The SJC held that although a Juvenile Court judge may act ex parte on an emergency custody petition, it was improper at the ensuing seventy-two hour hearing to rely on the unsworn social worker's petition and on facts the judge knew from earlier proceedings, and it remanded for a prompt new temporary custody hearing.
cases.quote: A judge in the Juvenile Court may conduct an ex parte hearing to determine whether to grant an emergency petition to obtain custody of a child.

relevance.INP-04: Zita limits what a judge may draw from her own prior involvement in related care and protection cases when deciding a new emergency petition.
relevance.INP-12: Zita confirms the two-step structure of Massachusetts protective custody: an ex parte emergency order followed by an evidentiary hearing within seventy-two hours.
relevance.DEC-04: The emergency custody decision may be made ex parte on the department's petition, but that unsworn petition cannot be used as evidence to extend custody at the next hearing.
relevance.ACT-03: A newborn's placement in departmental custody was vacated because the evidentiary record at the temporary custody hearing was improperly constituted.
relevance.FAIL-01: Zita is the SJC's template for vacating a temporary custody order obtained on improperly considered material, using G. L. c. 211, § 3.

cases.holding: The SJC held that children's out-of-court statements, though admissible against the children themselves as party-opponent statements, are not admissible against the parent who is contesting custody, and it reversed the temporary custody award to the department.
cases.quote: The statements of the children could not be admitted properly in evidence against the father.

relevance.DEC-02: Sophie governs what investigative product, specifically children's recorded statements, may be used against a parent once the department moves from investigation to court.
relevance.DEC-04: The abbreviated nature of a temporary custody hearing does not relax the rules of evidence that protect the parent's custodial interest.
relevance.ACT-03: A placement order resting on inadmissible child hearsay cannot stand, even as a temporary measure pending trial.

cases.holding: The SJC held that a care and protection petition is legally sufficient if it pleads specific facts, on knowledge or information and belief, falling within one of the four statutory grounds in G. L. c. 119, § 24, and that denial of emergency transfer of custody does not bar the petitioner from proceeding to a temporary custody hearing under § 25.
cases.quote: We conclude that a petition is sufficient if it contains allegations asserting specific facts, based on personal knowledge or information and belief, that fall within the statute’s enumerated concerns.

relevance.INP-12: Lillian separates the emergency-custody question from the underlying petition, so a refusal to remove immediately does not end the protective process.
relevance.DEC-04: A judge's finding of no immediate risk defeats emergency removal but leaves the § 25 temporary custody route open.
relevance.DEC-05: Lillian states the pleading standard a care and protection petition must meet before a Massachusetts court will open a dependency case.

cases.holding: The SJC held that where a Juvenile Court awards "permanent" custody of a nonmarital child to the father in a care and protection case, the Juvenile Court may keep the case open until a Probate and Family Court judge enters a custody order under G. L. c. 209C, and that this practice satisfies due process.
cases.quote: We agree that this practice best reflects the Legislature's intent and harmonizes the two statutory schemes.

relevance.INP-04: Jaylen maps the overlapping jurisdiction of the Juvenile Court and the Probate and Family Court over the same child, which determines which judge may order what.
relevance.OUT-01: Placement of the child with a fit parent does not by itself end the case; the Juvenile Court retains the case until a Probate and Family Court custody order issues.
relevance.OUT-04: Jaylen shows the durability of the custody order that will carry the child forward after the care and protection case finally closes.
relevance.OUT-05: A motion to dismiss and close the care and protection case was properly denied until the parallel c. 209C custody order was in place.

cases.holding: The SJC held that although impounded care and protection records carry a strong statutory privacy interest, a journalist showed good cause under Rule 7 of the Uniform Rules on Impoundment Procedure for release of audio recordings of hearings in the case of a child who was placed with her father without a completed ICPC home study and later went missing and died, and the judge abused her discretion in refusing release.
cases.quote: a person seeking access to impounded materials in a care and protection proceeding faces a high hurdle

relevance.INP-09: Adele is the Massachusetts vehicle by which outside scrutiny, here a documentary journalist, reaches a closed child welfare case and exposes systemic failure.
relevance.OUT-06: The case arises directly from a child's death after release from departmental custody and defines the public's access to the record of what the agency and courts did.
relevance.FAIL-03: The opinion documents the failure to obtain an Interstate Compact on the Placement of Children home study before interstate placement, a federal-compact compliance breakdown.
relevance.FAIL-04: Adele is the SJC's treatment of transparency where a child under agency supervision went missing and died after an interstate placement.
relevance.FAIL-06: Adele holds that statutory impoundment of child welfare records is not absolute and yields to a sufficient showing of good cause.
relevance.PMC-01: Adele shows the SJC weighing public accountability for departmental performance against the confidentiality that ordinarily shields that performance from review.

cases.holding: The SJC held that a trial judge's subsidiary findings stand unless clearly erroneous but the appellate court independently reviews whether those findings establish parental unfitness by clear and convincing evidence, and it reversed the Juvenile Court judgment placing the children in the department's permanent custody.
cases.quote: although the judge’s findings were not clearly erroneous, the evidence on which they were based did not prove parental unfitness by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.INP-02: The case opens with a § 51A report filed after a physician's examination and a mother's disclosure, showing how a third-party report becomes a custody case.
relevance.DEC-03: Eleanor distinguishes the facts an agency can prove from the legal conclusion of unfitness, which requires clear and convincing proof.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the proof falls short of clear and convincing evidence of unfitness, the custody judgment must be reversed and the children returned.
relevance.FAIL-01: Eleanor is the leading Massachusetts statement of the appellate standard used to overturn an agency-obtained custody determination.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed termination, holding that the department discharged its duty to strengthen and encourage the family unit where it worked diligently without success and the additional services the mother sought would not have solved her chronic problems, and that a court appointed special advocate appointed as guardian ad litem may testify and submit a report.
cases.quote: Mary’s argument that the department failed to fulfil its duty to strengthen and encourage the family unit lacks merit.

relevance.INP-04: Georgia authorizes the judge to appoint a CASA as guardian ad litem, an investigative resource the court itself sets in motion.
relevance.DEC-06: The opinion measures the adequacy of the service package the department offered in lieu of, and alongside, court compulsion.
relevance.ACT-01: Georgia holds that the duty to strengthen the family is satisfied by diligent effort, not by provision of every service a parent requests.
relevance.ACT-02: A parent's partial compliance with service plans does not defeat a finding of unfitness where no progress is made toward resuming care.
relevance.OUT-01: The reunification duty is measured by whether the services offered could realistically have solved the parent's chronic problems.
relevance.OUT-02: Georgia sustains a termination decree against a claim that the department's reasonable-efforts failure should have blocked it.
relevance.PMC-03: The court's endorsement of trained citizen volunteers (CASAs) as officers of the court is the closest Massachusetts analogue to structured citizen oversight of child welfare cases.

cases.holding: The SJC held that the department must make reasonable efforts to reunify before seeking termination, that a judge may weigh a failure of those efforts in deciding whether unfitness is merely temporary, but that a reasonable-efforts failure does not preclude an order in the child's best interest; it affirmed termination and left future visitation to the adoptive parents.
cases.quote: Before seeking to terminate parental rights, the department must make “reasonable efforts” aimed at restoring the child to the care of the natural parents.

relevance.DEC-06: Ilona defines the front-end service obligation that a differential or voluntary response is meant to satisfy before any petition is filed.
relevance.ACT-01: The reasonable-efforts duty attaches to the voluntary service plan stage and is the yardstick for whether the agency did enough short of court action.
relevance.ACT-02: Ilona holds that shortcomings in the department's court-ordered service provision do not automatically defeat a finding of unfitness.
relevance.OUT-01: Reasonable efforts "aimed at restoring the child to the care of the natural parents" is the Massachusetts formulation of the reunification duty.
relevance.OUT-02: A reasonable-efforts failure is relevant to whether unfitness is temporary but does not bar termination when the child's best interests require it.
relevance.FAIL-03: Ilona is the SJC's interpretation of the federal and state reasonable-efforts mandate, including the circumstances in which efforts are excused.
relevance.PMC-01: The reasonable-efforts finding is the judicial determination on which federal Title IV-E eligibility and CFSR performance measurement depend.

cases.holding: The SJC held that a judge in a termination proceeding may, and on the facts there should, enter visitation orders rather than leave all contact to the department and future adoptive parents, and remanded for explicit findings on both parental and sibling visitation.
cases.quote: That determination may lead or even require the judge to order post-termination or postadoption visitation in the first instance.

relevance.ACT-04: Rico requires the judge to address sibling contact explicitly rather than defer it to the agency and future caregivers.
relevance.OUT-02: Rico allocates to the court, not the department, the authority to secure a child's contact rights at the moment of termination.
relevance.OUT-03: The judge's visitation authority survives the transfer of custodial incidents to the department or to a permanent caregiver.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed the decree dispensing with the mother's consent to adoption and upheld the denial of visitation pending appeal, holding that the department proved unfitness by clear and convincing evidence and that posttermination visitation is governed by the child's best interests rather than by any independent parental right.
cases.quote: While posttermination visitation may be allowed, the proper focus is on the best interests of the child.

relevance.ACT-05: Helen confirms that an order cutting off a parent's contact with the child is measured by the same best-interests standard as a custody decision.
relevance.OUT-01: A parent seeking restoration of contact must proceed by review and redetermination under G. L. c. 119, § 26, on the child's best interests.
relevance.OUT-02: Helen rejects the argument that a judge must find affirmative harm before terminating visitation along with parental rights.

cases.holding: The SJC reversed the Appeals Court and upheld termination of the father's rights, holding that termination may be ordered even where it is not a necessary prerequisite to the children's permanency plans, so long as the judge finds it serves the children's best interests.
cases.quote: we conclude that termination may be ordered, even though termination is not a necessary prerequisite to a child’s permanency plan

relevance.OUT-02: Nancy answers whether a court may terminate when the permanency plan (here long-term placement) would not require it, and holds that it may.
relevance.OUT-03: The opinion addresses the "legal orphan" objection raised when permanency is achieved through guardianship or long-term care rather than adoption.
relevance.OUT-04: Nancy weighs the permanence and stability interests of older children whose plans do not culminate in adoption before they age out.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed the Juvenile Court judge's choice of the parents' plan for adoption by a paternal aunt over the department's plan for adoption by the foster mother, holding that the judge owes an even-handed assessment of competing plans and that his decision is entitled to substantial deference.
cases.quote: A judge should provide an “even handed” assessment of all the facts surrounding both the department’s plan and any competing custody or adoption plan.

relevance.ACT-04: Hugo is the leading Massachusetts authority for a court preferring a relative caregiver's plan over the agency's non-relative plan.
relevance.OUT-02: The judge, not the department, chooses among competing adoption plans, and the agency's preference carries no presumption.
relevance.OUT-03: Hugo governs the comparative evaluation of kinship and non-kinship permanency options.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed decrees terminating only the mother's rights, holding that a judge need not terminate both parents simultaneously and that the judge's findings adequately accounted for the geographic separation of the three siblings, whose relationship is weighed within the best-interests standard.
cases.quote: As a general matter, it may be preferable that siblings be raised together.

relevance.ACT-03: Willow addresses the placement decision that geographically separates siblings among different homes and states.
relevance.ACT-04: Sibling togetherness is a preference in Massachusetts placement law, but its weight varies with the circumstances of each child.
relevance.OUT-02: A termination decree is not invalid merely because it separates siblings or leaves the other parent's rights intact.

cases.case_name: Lindsay v. Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The SJC clarified that on judicial review of a "supported" finding of abuse or neglect, the court asks only whether substantial evidence supports the hearing officer's conclusion that there was reasonable cause to believe the maltreatment occurred, and it upheld the supported finding of neglect.
cases.quote: there need only be “substantial evidence” supporting the conclusion that there was “reasonable cause to believe” that Lindsay neglected Adrianna

relevance.INP-02: Lindsay arises from a third-party report of neglect at a day care center and traces it through investigation to a supported finding.
relevance.INP-06: The "reasonable cause to believe" threshold Lindsay construes is the same low standard that governs intake and screening decisions.
relevance.INP-10: The opinion explains how a report is escalated to a § 51B investigation and how the resulting finding is reviewed.
relevance.DEC-01: Lindsay identifies what an agency must have before it may support rather than screen out or unfound an allegation.
relevance.DEC-02: The standard Lindsay sets is the outcome measure against which the adequacy of the § 51B investigation is judged.
relevance.DEC-03: Lindsay is the controlling SJC authority on the proof required for, and the judicial review of, a substantiated ("supported") finding in Massachusetts.

cases.case_name: Magazu v. Department of Children and Families
cases.holding: The SJC upheld the department's denial of a foster and preadoptive parent application based on the applicants' religiously motivated use of corporal punishment on their own children, holding the decision was supported by substantial evidence and that the substantial burden on the applicants' religious exercise was outweighed by the Commonwealth's compelling interest in protecting foster children.
cases.quote: Consistent with this compelling State interest, the department has determined that a foster child should not be placed in a home where corporal punishment is used as a disciplinary measure.

relevance.ACT-03: Magazu is the SJC's statement of the department's authority to set and apply foster-home licensing standards that control where a child may be placed.
relevance.FAIL-05: Magazu is the leading Massachusetts decision rejecting a religious-discrimination challenge to a foster placement licensing denial, and it supplies the framework any such claim must meet.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed an order authorizing physicians to give blood transfusions to a child over her parents' religious objection, holding that where the child's life is threatened by the parental refusal, the interests of the child and the State outweigh the parents' right to refuse treatment.
cases.quote: We conclude that the interests of Elisha and of the State outweigh her parents’ rights to refuse the medical treatment.

relevance.INP-07: The hospital's petition is the paradigm medical-setting trigger for state protective intervention short of removal.
relevance.ACT-06: McCauley is the controlling Massachusetts authority for judicially authorized emergency medical treatment of a child over parental objection.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed an adjudication that a child with acute lymphocytic leukemia was in need of care and protection and an order directing chemotherapy over the parents' objection, holding that the order was consistent with the child's best interests and the State's interests and did not violate the parents' constitutional rights.
cases.quote: the decision below was consistent with both the best interests of the child and the applicable interests of the State

relevance.INP-07: The case begins with treating physicians reporting the parents' abandonment of medically indicated treatment, the classic medical-disclosure trigger.
relevance.ACT-06: This is the foundational Massachusetts decision authorizing court-ordered life-saving medical treatment through the care and protection statute.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed entry of a substituted judgment "do not resuscitate" order for a child in the department's custody who was in a persistent vegetative state, holding that the State's general interest in preserving life is not absolute and yields where the issue is only how briefly life may be extended.
cases.quote: The substituted judgment decision and the entry of the “do not resuscitate” order are affirmed.

relevance.ACT-06: Beth is the Massachusetts authority for judicial authorization of end-of-life medical decisions for a child in agency custody.
relevance.OUT-06: Beth governs the court's role when a child under the department's supervision suffers catastrophic injury and death is imminent.
relevance.FAIL-04: The opinion shows the judicial oversight required before the agency may make a life-ending care decision for a child it holds in custody.
relevance.PMC-04: Beth is the closest Massachusetts authority on the judicial process that must precede and document decisions about a dying child in state care.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed a care and protection judgment committing a child to the Department of Public Welfare, holding that the absence of an express finding of general parental unfitness did not require reversal where the subsidiary findings were tantamount to unfitness as to this child's welfare, and that the child's wishes were properly given weight.
cases.quote: The failure of the trial judge to make an express finding of general parental unfitness also does not warrant a reversal in this case.

relevance.INP-08: The case originates in a fifth-grade teacher's observations of behavior problems, absenteeism and the child's complaints, which produced the investigation.
relevance.DEC-03: The decision explains what findings suffice to establish unfitness in relation to a particular child even without a general unfitness label.

cases.holding: The SJC held that an indigent parent is entitled to appointed counsel in a private guardianship proceeding concerning her child, reasoning that the parent's liberty interest does not depend on whether the State is a party.
cases.quote: There is no reason why an indigent parent whose child is the subject of a guardianship proceeding should receive the benefit of counsel only if the State is involved.

relevance.INP-05: V.V. addresses the private, non-agency route by which a child's custody changes hands and holds that the parent's protections travel with it.
relevance.OUT-03: V.V. is the SJC's foundational holding on counsel for indigent parents in guardianship permanency proceedings.

cases.holding: The SJC held that a guardian who is a de facto parent has no liberty interest supporting a procedural due process right to counsel in a removal proceeding, but that the Probate and Family Court's equitable powers permit a judge to appoint counsel for an indigent guardian where the child's best interests warrant it.
cases.quote: A guardian who is a de facto parent does not have a liberty interest in her relationship with her ward sufficient to warrant the appointment of counsel.

relevance.INP-05: K.N. defines the standing and procedural protections of a non-parent caregiver who has assumed the parenting role by private arrangement.
relevance.ACT-04: K.N. governs the legal position of a kin or de facto caregiver whose guardianship the agency or a parent later seeks to undo.
relevance.OUT-03: K.N. distinguishes the constitutional entitlements of parents from the equitable, discretionary protections available to guardians in permanency proceedings.

cases.case_name: People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, Inc. v. Department of Agricultural Resources
cases.holding: The SJC construed the public safety and privacy exemptions to the public records law, holding that the statutes favor disclosure by presuming records are public and placing on the custodian the burden of proving with specificity that an exemption applies.
cases.quote: Together, these statutes, and our cases interpreting them, favor disclosure of public records in two primary ways.

relevance.INP-09: PETA supplies the doctrinal presumption that lets oversight bodies and the public obtain state agency records.
relevance.FAIL-03: The opinion sets the standard a state agency must satisfy to withhold records that would reveal its own compliance record.
relevance.FAIL-06: PETA holds that the custodian must prove an exemption with specificity; generalized assertions of harm are insufficient.
relevance.PMC-02: PETA is the SJC's framework for obtaining the financial and programmatic records that audits depend on.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review of agency performance depends on the disclosure presumption PETA articulates.
relevance.PMC-05: PETA is the leading modern SJC statement of the Massachusetts public records law's pro-disclosure structure.
relevance.PMC-06: Systematic data collection from Massachusetts agencies operates within the presumption and exemption scheme PETA describes.

cases.holding: The SJC held that the Juvenile Court properly exercised jurisdiction to adjudicate a child in need of care and protection and to dispense with the consent of a father who was a foreign national in the United States on a temporary work visa, and affirmed the finding of unfitness as overwhelmingly supported.
cases.quote: We conclude that the Juvenile Court properly exercised jurisdiction and now affirm the decree.

relevance.INP-11: Peggy is the Massachusetts answer to a jurisdictional objection based on the parent's and child's foreign nationality and immigration status.
relevance.DEC-05: Jurisdiction to open a care and protection case does not depend on the citizenship or immigration status of the parent or child.
relevance.FAIL-05: Peggy rejects the contention that a parent's foreign nationality limits the court's authority, while requiring the same clear and convincing proof of unfitness as in any other case.

cases.case_name: Kyle K. v. Department of Children and Families
cases.holding: The Appeals Court upheld a DCF hearing officer's decision affirming a "supported" finding of sexual abuse, holding that judicial review under G. L. c. 30A asks only whether substantial evidence supports the conclusion that there was reasonable cause to believe the abuse occurred, with particular deference to the hearing officer's credibility determinations.
cases.quote: As to facts, where there is substantial evidence to support the findings of the agency, the court will not substitute its own view of the facts.

relevance.INP-01: The opinion sets out the mandated reporter's § 51A duty to notify DCF on reasonable cause to believe a child is suffering abuse, and traces what follows.
relevance.INP-06: Kyle K. shows the sequence from report through § 51B investigation to a supported finding, and the deferential review that attaches at the end.
relevance.INP-08: Statements relayed by the child's school guidance counselor were part of the record the hearing officer weighed.
relevance.INP-10: The opinion describes DCF's obligation to investigate under § 51B once a report meets the reasonable-cause threshold.
relevance.DEC-01: The hearing officer reversed the physical abuse allegation while sustaining the sexual abuse allegation, illustrating allegation-by-allegation unfounding.
relevance.DEC-03: Kyle K. is the most recent Massachusetts appellate statement of what "supported" means and how little evidence sustains it on review.
relevance.FAIL-01: Kyle K. defines the narrow grounds on which a court will set aside a DCF hearing officer's decision.

cases.case_name: B.K. v. Department of Children & Families
cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed DCF's supported finding of emotional neglect where the father repeatedly violated a Probate and Family Court order barring contact with his daughter, holding that substantial evidence supported the hearing officer's reasonable-cause determination while cautioning that emotional neglect does not follow automatically whenever a parent prioritizes his own needs.
cases.quote: Our task on appeal is to determine whether there was substantial evidence to support DCF’s decision that there was reasonable cause to believe the father was responsible for neglect.

relevance.INP-08: The father's delivery of a letter to his daughter through her school principal was the conduct that produced the neglect finding.
relevance.INP-10: The case follows a § 51A report through DCF investigation to a supported finding of emotional neglect.
relevance.DEC-03: B.K. is the Massachusetts appellate authority defining emotional neglect as a supported finding and the evidence needed to sustain it.
relevance.ACT-05: B.K. shows how violation of a civil no-contact order entered in the Probate and Family Court becomes the basis of a child protection finding.
relevance.FAIL-01: The opinion states the substantial evidence test that a parent must overcome to reverse a DCF finding in court.

cases.case_name: C.M. v. Commissioner of the Department of Children and Families
cases.holding: The Appeals Court held that DCF workers have absolute immunity for deciding to initiate care and protection proceedings and for their testimony, but only qualified immunity for their investigations and for factual assertions sworn on personal knowledge in an affidavit supporting a removal petition; it vacated summary judgment on the § 1983 claim based on the allegedly false affidavit.
cases.quote: In sum, DCF workers are protected by absolute immunity in their decisions to initiate care and protection proceedings and in testifying at the subsequent hearings or trials on the petitions.

relevance.INP-03: The opinion addresses the interaction of DCF's safety planning with information about a registered sex offender's access to the child.
relevance.ACT-01: C.M. holds that DCF's authority is bounded by G. L. c. 119, §§ 24-29, and that a voluntary safety plan cannot itself create a basis for later action.
relevance.DEC-04: A social worker who swears a false affidavit to obtain ex parte emergency custody acts as a complaining witness and is not absolutely immune.
relevance.DEC-05: The decision to file the care and protection petition is prosecutorial and absolutely immune; the supporting factual affidavit is not.
relevance.FAIL-02: C.M. is the controlling Massachusetts appellate authority on § 1983 damages liability for a wrongful removal obtained through a false affidavit.

cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed a temporary custody order, holding that social worker affidavits filed with the petition are not categorically inadmissible at the seventy-two hour hearing but are admissible only to the extent permitted by Adoption of Luc, that unpreserved hearsay objections are waived, and that the judge did not deny the father due process by intermittently muting his participation in a remote hearing.
cases.quote: The judge acted within her discretion, and within constitutional bounds, in intermittently limiting the father's participation at the hearing, which took place through an Internet-based video conferencing platform.

relevance.INP-12: Doretta applies the Robert fair-preponderance standard to the continuation of protective custody after emergency removal.
relevance.ACT-02: The parents' refusal to obtain and accept offered services supported the finding that the children could not safely be returned.
relevance.ACT-03: Doretta is the most recent published Massachusetts appellate guidance on the evidence that will sustain a foster placement at the temporary custody stage.
relevance.DEC-04: Doretta governs the use of social worker affidavits and hearsay at the hearing that decides whether an emergency removal continues.
relevance.PMC-01: The opinion illustrates the judicial checks Massachusetts applies at the earliest stage of agency custody, the stage federal reviews measure for timeliness and quality.

cases.holding: The Appeals Court held that claims of ineffective assistance of counsel in care and protection and adoption proceedings, including claims by children against their own appointed counsel, are measured by the Saferian standard, and it reviewed the denial of the children's Rule 60(b)(6) motion for a new trial under that framework.
cases.quote: Claims of ineffective assistance of counsel in care and protection and adoption proceedings are measured by the standards set forth in Commonwealth v. Saferian

relevance.FAIL-01: Georgette is the Appeals Court's statement of the test for vacating a care and protection or termination judgment because of deficient representation, including representation of the child.

cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed a termination decree over an Indian Child Welfare Act challenge, holding that the department satisfied 25 U.S.C. § 1912(a) notice where the three federally recognized Cherokee tribes responded that the child was not an "Indian child," and rejecting the related reasonable-efforts and unfitness claims.
cases.quote: These responsive letters from the three Cherokee tribes demonstrate that the department in fact did comply with ICWA notice provision.

relevance.INP-11: Uday is the only Massachusetts appellate decision located that reaches an ICWA issue, and it governs the department's notice obligation when a child may have tribal ancestry.

cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed the judge's acceptance of DCF's adoption plan and his refusal to order postadoption parental visitation, but remanded because the judge declined to set any schedule for sibling visitation among children adopted into separate homes.
cases.quote: we remand for the judge to provide a schedule for post-termination and postadoption sibling visitation

relevance.ACT-04: Zander requires an enforceable sibling contact schedule when siblings are dispersed among different adoptive families.
relevance.ACT-05: The judge's order prohibiting all contact between the biological father and the child illustrates a protective no-contact order entered within a permanency decree.
relevance.OUT-02: Zander distinguishes parental visitation, which may be left to adoptive parents, from sibling visitation, which the judge must address.
relevance.OUT-03: The decision governs the contact arrangements that must accompany permanency for siblings placed apart.

cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed termination, holding that homelessness, poverty and financial instability cannot alone support termination but may properly be considered as part of the unfitness determination where they are tied to the parent's inability to provide minimally adequate care.
cases.quote: While homelessness, poverty, and financial instability alone are not sufficient to terminate a person's parental rights, they are proper considerations in an unfitness determination.

relevance.INP-01: The case begins with a pediatrician's § 51A report of neglect, a mandated reporter's disclosure in a medical setting.
relevance.INP-07: Virgil illustrates how a treating physician's observations become the § 51A report that opens the case.
relevance.DEC-01: Virgil marks the line between conditions of poverty, which do not by themselves justify intervention, and parenting deficits that do.
relevance.DEC-03: The opinion states the required nexus between a parent's circumstances and a risk of harm before a maltreatment finding or unfitness determination may rest on them.
relevance.OUT-02: Virgil is the Massachusetts authority limiting the weight of poverty and homelessness in a termination decision.
relevance.FAIL-05: Virgil is the closest Massachusetts appellate guard against terminating parental rights on grounds that are effectively economic status.

cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed termination and held that, on the limited circumstances presented, a judge could order the mother's drug rehabilitation program to produce an affidavit explaining her departure, because the children's best interests outweighed her confidentiality interest in treatment information.
cases.quote: We conclude that under the limited circumstances of this case, the best interests of the children outweigh the mother's right to confidentiality in information concerning her treatment.

relevance.DEC-02: Lisette governs when an investigating agency or court may reach otherwise confidential substance-use treatment records in a child protection case.
relevance.FAIL-06: Lisette shows that confidentiality protections in child welfare litigation are balanced, not absolute, and yield on a case-specific showing.
relevance.PMC-05: The decision marks the boundary between individual privacy in treatment records and the disclosure required for child protection decision making.

cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed judgment for the Commonwealth and for the individual social workers on a former foster child's claims arising from her placement with a man who abused her, holding among other things that the workers had qualified immunity because the asserted right to safety in a relative placement was not clearly established at the time.
cases.quote: The plaintiff’s placement with a relative, rather than in foster care, further supports the conclusion that she has not asserted a right that was clearly established.

relevance.ACT-04: Sheila S. is the Massachusetts decision analyzing agency liability for placing a child with a purported relative without verifying his circumstances.
relevance.OUT-06: The case sets out what a child harmed while under agency supervision must prove to recover against the Commonwealth and its workers.
relevance.FAIL-04: Sheila S. is the leading Massachusetts appellate treatment of damages claims for serious harm suffered by a child in departmental custody.
relevance.PMC-04: The opinion illustrates how limitations periods and immunity doctrines constrain after-the-fact accountability for harm to children in state care.

cases.case_name: Gallagher v. South Shore Hospital, Inc.
cases.holding: The Appeals Court held that a protective services caseworker and a police officer who entered a home during an abuse investigation without a warrant, consent, court order, or a reasonable belief of an emergency could be found to have violated the Fourth Amendment and art. 14, and that no community caretaking exception permits entry into a home.
cases.quote: there cannot be a community caretaking exception permitting entry into the home under art. 14 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights

relevance.INP-03: Gallagher involves a joint entry by a protective services caseworker and a police officer, the standard co-response posture in abuse investigations.
relevance.INP-12: The opinion holds that the urge to protect a vulnerable person does not by itself supply the emergency justification needed to enter a home.
relevance.DEC-02: Gallagher is the closest published Massachusetts appellate authority on the constitutional limits of a protective services caseworker's home entry during an investigation.
relevance.FAIL-02: The decision supplies the Massachusetts constitutional framework, and the qualified immunity analysis, for damages claims arising from an unlawful protective entry and seizure.

cases.case_name: Hatch v. Department for Children, Youth & Their Families
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: The First Circuit affirmed denial of leave to amend as futile, holding that a child protective official who removes a child on an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse does not violate clearly established law and is entitled to qualified immunity notwithstanding the parent's right to family integrity.
cases.quote: Because the welfare of the child is paramount, an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse justifies protective measures.

relevance.INP-12: Hatch fixes the constitutional threshold, objectively reasonable suspicion, for taking a child into protective custody in the First Circuit.
relevance.DEC-04: The emergency removal decision is measured against what the worker reasonably believed at the time, not against what later proved true.
relevance.FAIL-02: Hatch is the governing First Circuit qualified immunity authority for § 1983 wrongful-removal claims arising in Massachusetts.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: The First Circuit affirmed summary judgment for social workers and private child protection agencies sued under § 1983 by a Massachusetts father over their role in a sexual abuse investigation, holding that the familial-integrity right is too fact-dependent and unsettled to have been clearly established and that litigation communications were privileged.
cases.quote: Because this interest must always be balanced against the governmental interest involved, it is difficult, if not impossible, for officials to know when they have violated “clearly established” law.

relevance.DEC-02: Frazier addresses the constitutional exposure of investigators, public and private, who conduct and act on a child sexual abuse investigation in Massachusetts.
relevance.FAIL-02: Frazier is the First Circuit's Massachusetts-based statement of why familial-integrity claims usually founder on the clearly-established prong of qualified immunity.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that before a State may irrevocably terminate parental rights, due process requires proof of at least clear and convincing evidence, and it reversed a judgment entered under a fair preponderance standard.
cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

relevance.DEC-03: Santosky supplies the federal constitutional floor for the proof that must support the state's allegations before parental rights are severed.
relevance.OUT-02: Santosky is the controlling federal authority requiring clear and convincing evidence in every termination of parental rights proceeding.
relevance.FAIL-01: A judgment terminating parental rights on less than clear and convincing evidence is constitutionally infirm and must be set aside.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding and left the question to case-by-case determination by the trial court, affirming the judgment against the unrepresented mother.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: Lassiter is the federal baseline on appointed counsel in termination cases, a floor that Massachusetts exceeds by statute under G. L. c. 119, § 29.
relevance.FAIL-01: Lassiter frames the federal due process claim available when a parent proceeded without counsel, and explains why Massachusetts practice provides greater protection.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a State may not take children from a parent without a hearing on that parent's fitness, and struck down Illinois' presumption that unmarried fathers are unfit.
cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

relevance.INP-12: Stanley is the source of the constitutional requirement that a fitness hearing follow any state removal of a child from a parent.
relevance.DEC-04: An emergency removal must be followed promptly by a hearing at which the parent's fitness is actually adjudicated.
relevance.DEC-05: The petition that opens a dependency case must lead to an individualized fitness determination, not a categorical presumption.
relevance.FAIL-02: Stanley is the foundational federal authority for the proposition that removing a child without an individualized fitness hearing violates due process.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court rejected all challenges to the Indian Child Welfare Act, holding that Congress had authority to enact it, that its placement preferences and active-efforts provisions do not violate the anticommandeering doctrine, and that the equal protection and nondelegation claims failed for lack of standing.
cases.quote: we reject all of petitioners’ challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: Brackeen confirms that ICWA's jurisdictional, active-efforts and placement-preference requirements bind Massachusetts state courts in any proceeding involving an Indian child.
relevance.FAIL-03: Brackeen establishes that a state court's failure to apply ICWA is a failure to comply with valid federal law, not merely with policy.

cases.case_name: Covell v. Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The SJC affirmed the department's decision to "support" an allegation of sexual abuse and to list the plaintiff in its registry of alleged perpetrators, holding that a supported finding requires only reasonable cause to believe the abuse occurred, that the substantial evidence test does not become more stringent because the consequences of the agency decision are severe, and that hearsay bearing indicia of reliability can by itself be substantial evidence.
cases.quote: Substantial evidence may be based on hearsay alone if that hearsay has "indicia of reliability."

relevance.INP-08: The case begins with a school guidance counsellor's G. L. c. 119, § 51A report of suspected sexual abuse, the paradigm educational-setting disclosure.
relevance.DEC-01: Covell fixes what the department must have before it may support rather than unsupport an allegation: reasonable cause to believe, not proof that the abuse in fact occurred.
relevance.DEC-03: Covell is the leading SJC authority on what a "supported" finding requires and on substantial-evidence review of a DCF fair-hearing decision, the case Lindsay, Kyle K. and B.K. all build on.

cases.holding: The SJC held that the good cause standard of Rule 7 of the Uniform Rules on Impoundment Procedure governs requests by the parties or the Commonwealth for access to impounded care and protection records, that the proponent of release bears the burden of establishing good cause, and that a parent's decision to testify and to waive the psychotherapist privilege at the care and protection trial does not waive either at a later criminal trial; it remanded for application of that standard.
cases.quote: a party or the Commonwealth seeking to pierce this veil of privacy should bear the burden of demonstrating good cause for release from impoundment

relevance.INP-09: M.C. I establishes the mechanism by which an outside actor can reach the sealed record of a child welfare case, the precondition for any external review of what the agency did.
relevance.FAIL-06: M.C. I holds that statutory impoundment of care and protection records is not absolute and that release turns on a balancing of the enumerated Rule 7 good cause factors.
relevance.PMC-05: M.C. I is the source of the Massachusetts good-cause framework governing disclosure of otherwise-confidential child welfare records, the framework Care and Protection of Adele later applies to a journalist.

cases.holding: On review after remand, the SJC affirmed the Juvenile Court's partial release of impounded care and protection records to the father and the Commonwealth but vacated so much of the order as released the mother's testimony and her psychotherapist's testimony to the Commonwealth, holding that concerns of trial efficiency alone cannot establish good cause where the privilege against self-incrimination and the patient-psychotherapist privilege are both implicated.
cases.quote: This concern, alone, does not serve to tip the balance toward release from impoundment where the mother's Fifth Amendment rights and the patient-psychotherapist privilege are both at play.

relevance.INP-09: M.C. II shows the good cause factors actually applied document by document, which is the practical measure of how far an outside reviewer can see into a care and protection file.
relevance.FAIL-06: M.C. II confirms that release or withholding must rest on the Rule 7 factors, and that a judge who substitutes considerations of convenience for that balance errs.
relevance.PMC-05: M.C. II marks the outer limit of disclosure: privileged testimony stays impounded absent a showing that outweighs the privilege asserted.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed the judgment dispensing with the parents' consent to adoption, holding that a proceeding to terminate parental rights is not a "service, program, or activity" so the Americans with Disabilities Act may not be raised as a defense to it, while holding that the ADA, Massachusetts antidiscrimination law and the State Constitution do require the department to accommodate a disabled parent's special needs in the services it provides beforehand, and that the department did so here.
cases.quote: the ADA, as well as Massachusetts anti-discrimination laws, regulations, and our Constitution all require the department to accommodate the parents' special needs in its provision of services

relevance.ACT-01: Gregory measures the front-end service package against the department's duty to accommodate a parent's cognitive disability before any court action is sought.
relevance.ACT-02: A disabled parent who believes court-ordered services are not accommodating the disability must say so when the service plan is adopted or shortly after, not for the first time at the termination trial.
relevance.FAIL-05: Gregory is the leading Massachusetts authority on disability discrimination in child welfare: the ADA is no defense to termination, but the department must accommodate a disabled parent in the services it renders.

cases.holding: The SJC reversed a Probate and Family Court judgment denying a mother's petition to remove the guardian and regain custody of her two children, holding that the findings were inadequate because unfitness must be predicated on parental behavior that adversely affects the child and there was no evidence in the record connecting the mother's lesbian household to her fitness as a parent.
cases.quote: A finding that a parent is unfit to further the welfare of the child must be predicated upon parental behavior which adversely affects the child.

relevance.DEC-01: Bezio draws the line between a parent's status or household arrangement, which cannot by itself justify state intervention, and behavior that demonstrably harms the child, which can.
relevance.FAIL-05: Bezio is the foundational Massachusetts holding that a parent's lifestyle or status cannot support a custody deprivation absent a demonstrated nexus to harm to the child.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed the denial of the children's Mass. R. Civ. P. 60(b)(6) motion for a new trial, holding that the Saferian standard governs ineffective-assistance claims in care and protection proceedings, that counsel's joint representation of siblings created no actual conflict and no prejudice was shown given overwhelming proof of the father's unfitness, and directing that counsel for children follow the 1999 CPCS performance standards on representing a child's expressed preferences.
cases.quote: their positions, based on mature expression, are entitled to weight in custody proceedings (although not determinative)

relevance.INP-04: Georgette sets out when a child's appointed counsel should ask the court to appoint a guardian ad litem, the judicially ordered investigative step available when counsel and child diverge.
relevance.OUT-05: A child dissatisfied with the resulting custody judgment may seek relief under rule 60(b)(6), but must show both deficient representation and prejudice before the judgment will be undone.

cases.holding: The SJC dismissed as moot a mother's G. L. c. 211, § 3 appeal from an order treating her non-appearance as a waiver of the seventy-two hour hearing, the Juvenile Court having vacated that order and held the hearing, and stated that the hearing exists to determine whether the child would be in immediate danger of serious abuse or neglect if returned and that continuances sought to delay it for a parent's own benefit are properly denied.
cases.quote: whether a child will be in immediate danger of serious abuse or neglect if returned to his parents or custodian

relevance.INP-12: Perry states the substantive question the seventy-two hour hearing answers, the question to which Robert's fair-preponderance burden of proof attaches.
relevance.DEC-04: Perry supplies the operative test at the hearing that decides whether an emergency removal continues, and holds that such hearings must be held as promptly as possible.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed a judgment dispensing with the mother's consent to the adoption of her two children, holding that the court investigator's reports were properly admitted and incorporated into the judge's findings, that those findings were not clearly erroneous, and that the mother's postadoption-visitation and ineffective-assistance claims were not preserved at trial and presented no exceptional circumstances warranting appellate review.
cases.quote: Generally, issues not raised by a losing party in the trial court are not addressed on appeal, absent exceptional circumstances.

relevance.DEC-02: Mary holds that the court investigator's report, the product of the judicially ordered investigation, is admissible and may be incorporated into the judge's findings in a c. 210 proceeding as well as in care and protection.
relevance.FAIL-01: Mary is the SJC authority that a parent who failed to raise an issue at trial, including ineffective assistance of counsel, ordinarily cannot obtain reversal on it, which defines the practical limits of appellate relief from an agency-obtained judgment.

cases.holding: The SJC reversed the Appeals Court and reinstated the orders terminating the mother's parental rights, holding that the trial judge did properly consider whether her unfitness was temporary, that a condition reasonably likely to continue for a prolonged, indeterminate period is not a temporary condition, and that termination was not an abuse of discretion.
cases.quote: A judge may say "enough" when faced with an indeterminate period of time required for parental recovery, if recovery is a viable possibility.

relevance.ACT-02: Elena qualifies the court-ordered service analysis: a parent's theoretical prospect of benefiting from more services does not forestall termination when the time to recovery is indeterminate.
relevance.OUT-02: Elena is the SJC's statement of when unfitness is not merely temporary, the operative limit on the reasonable-efforts argument the brief otherwise takes from Ilona.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed the finding that the mother was currently unfit by clear and convincing evidence but vacated the order committing the three sisters permanently to the department and remanded, because the judge's findings failed to address the importance of the sibling relationship and whether placing all three children with their paternal grandparents would serve their best interests.
cases.quote: The courts of this Commonwealth have recognized the importance of siblings' being raised together.

relevance.ACT-04: Three Minors is the source of the Massachusetts sibling-togetherness preference that Willow and Zander apply, and it requires findings on a proposed kinship placement of all the siblings together.
relevance.OUT-03: A permanency disposition that scatters siblings and passes over an available grandparent placement cannot stand without findings addressing both.

cases.holding: The SJC affirmed a Probate and Family Court judgment awarding the father custody of his daughter but ordering continuing visitation between the child and the maternal aunt who had been her guardian and de facto parent, holding that the judge's reliance on the child's best interests was appropriate and fell within the court's general equity jurisdiction notwithstanding the absence of any statute authorizing visitation for an aunt or former guardian.
cases.quote: The judge's consideration of Tamika's best interests was entirely appropriate.

relevance.INP-05: Youmans concerns the private guardianship route by which a relative becomes a child's parent in fact, and what protections the child retains when a legal parent later reclaims custody.
relevance.ACT-04: Youmans establishes that a kin caregiver who has become the child's de facto parent may be given court-ordered continuing contact even after custody passes to a legal parent.
relevance.OUT-03: Youmans is the SJC's foundational treatment of de facto parenthood and of the Probate and Family Court's equitable authority to preserve the child's relationship with a former guardian, the companion to Guardianship of K.N.

cases.case_name: Petition of Dept. of Public Welfare
cases.holding: The SJC affirmed two Probate Court decrees dispensing with parental consent to the adoption of two children, holding that the judge applied the correct statutory standard and based the decrees on a proper assessment of all the relevant facts, while agreeing that the State must make every effort to strengthen and encourage family life before it moves to sever family ties permanently.
cases.quote: we agree that the State is required to make every effort to strengthen and encourage family life before it may proceed with plans to sever family ties permanently

relevance.ACT-01: This is the original Massachusetts statement of the duty to strengthen and encourage family life, the obligation a voluntary service plan is meant to discharge.
relevance.DEC-06: The duty to try to preserve the family first is the doctrinal basis for engaging a family with services instead of filing a petition.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification in Massachusetts rests on the State's obligation to make every effort to strengthen family life before permanent severance is even considered.

cases.case_name: In Re the Department of Public Welfare to Dispense With Consent to Adoption
cases.holding: The SJC reversed a judgment dispensing with a mother's consent to the adoption of her child and remanded for further proceedings, holding that the judgment was unsupported by adequate findings as to the fitness of the surviving parent and emphasizing the recognized developmental risks that disruption of the parent-child relationship carries.
cases.quote: there exists a "substantial and impressive consensus" among experts in the field of child development that "disruption of the parent-child relationship carries significant risks" for the child

relevance.ACT-01: The opinion grounds the department's duty to strengthen and encourage families in the demonstrated developmental harm that separation itself inflicts on a child.
relevance.ACT-02: The decision holds the department to its own regulations and to the Commonwealth's declared family-preservation policy when it provides services under court supervision.
relevance.DEC-06: The recognized risks of separation are the reason Massachusetts law prefers service provision short of a petition wherever safety permits.

cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed a decree terminating the mother's parental rights, holding that a deceased DCF social worker's dictation notes and reports were admissible both as official records and as the declaration of a decedent, subject to the conditions that they be limited or redacted to facts rather than opinion, diagnosis or evaluation and that the author be available for cross-examination on request, and that second-level hearsay within them is admissible with opinion material edited out.
cases.quote: The dictation notes and the reports were admissible subject to two conditions.

relevance.DEC-02: Luc states the conditions on which the product of DCF's investigation - case work documents, dictation notes and reports - may be used as evidence against a parent.
relevance.DEC-03: Luc supplies the hearsay rule that Care and Protection of Doretta applies when it measures what a social worker's affidavit or report may actually prove; citing Doretta without Luc cites the application without the rule.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that the "reasonable efforts" clause of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act of 1980 confers no federally enforceable right on the children it benefits and creates no implied private cause of action, leaving compliance to be enforced by the Secretary of Health and Human Services through the state-plan approval and funding process.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.FAIL-03: Suter holds that a State's failure to make reasonable efforts is a matter for federal administrative enforcement against the State's funding, not a claim private plaintiffs may bring.
relevance.PMC-01: Suter explains why CFSR-style federal review by HHS, rather than private litigation, is the mechanism that polices a State's Title IV-E performance.
relevance.PMC-02: Suter is the controlling federal authority locating child-welfare funding compliance in the Secretary's plan-approval and audit powers, the legal foundation of OIG and Single Audit Act review; no Massachusetts or First Circuit decision on those programs was located.

cases.case_name: United States Department of Justice v. Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that FOIA Exemption 7(C) categorically protects an FBI criminal-history "rap sheet" from disclosure to a third-party requester, because the privacy interest in the practical obscurity of compiled information outweighs a public interest that FOIA measures only by what the record would reveal about the government's own conduct.
cases.quote: Official information that sheds light on an agency's performance of its statutory duties falls squarely within that statutory purpose.

relevance.FAIL-06: Reporters Committee defines the only public interest that counts under FOIA - what the record shows about the agency's own performance - which is precisely the interest asserted when an agency withholds its child welfare data.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the controlling federal statement of FOIA's purpose and of the privacy limits on it; no Massachusetts or First Circuit decision construing FOIA in a child welfare context was located.
relevance.PMC-06: Reporters Committee holds that aggregating individually obtainable records into a compilation creates a privacy interest of its own, the central legal constraint on systematic data collection across agency records.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener in this session (search + full opinion text) and the quoted language was verified programmatically as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after whitespace normalization. All quotes are from majority/lead opinions; none is from a syllabus, headnote, dissent or concurrence. Care & Protection of Beth's quoted disposition was checked to confirm it precedes the Nolan, J., dissent.

Reporter citations: the CourtListener cluster records for Kyle K. v. Department of Children and Families, C.M. v. Commissioner, Adoption of Uday, Care and Protection of Adele, Care and Protection of Jaylen, Adoption of Lisette and Mack v. District Attorney contained no reporter citation, so those entries use slip form with the docket number taken from the opinion's own caption. The one exception is Adoption of Lisette, cited as 93 Mass. App. Ct. 284 (2018) because that official citation appears in the text of Care and Protection of Doretta, which was retrieved and read in this session. Practitioners should confirm the current official citations for the six slip-form entries before filing.

ICWA (INP-11): no published Massachusetts appellate decision applying ICWA's active-efforts requirement, qualified expert witness requirement, placement preferences, or transfer-to-tribal-court provisions was located, and no Massachusetts state-ICWA statute was found. Adoption of Uday (notice under 25 U.S.C. section 1912(a)) is the only Massachusetts appellate decision located that reaches an ICWA issue; Haaland v. Brackeen supplies the federal standard. This is a genuine gap in Massachusetts case law, not a gap in the search.

Extended foster care / jurisdiction past 18 (OUT-04): no Massachusetts appellate authority construing extended foster care or continued jurisdiction past age eighteen was located. Care & Protection of Erin is mapped because the SJC dismissed the appeal as moot the moment the child turned eighteen, which is itself the operative Massachusetts rule on the outer edge of Juvenile Court care and protection jurisdiction; Adoption of Nancy and Care and Protection of Jaylen address permanency for older youth. This node is thinly supported and should be treated as unresolved in Massachusetts case law.

Fourth Amendment entry by a child protective caseworker (DEC-02, INP-12, FAIL-02): no published Massachusetts appellate decision was located applying the Fourth Amendment or art. 14 to a DCF caseworker's entry into a home during a G. L. c. 119, section 51B investigation. Gallagher v. South Shore Hospital is the closest published Massachusetts authority - same Commonwealth, a protective services caseworker entering a home with a police officer - but it arises under the elder protective services statute, G. L. c. 19A, not c. 119. It is included on that basis and should be cited as analogous, not controlling, in a child welfare case. The First Circuit cases (Hatch, Frazier, Watterson) supply the section 1983 framework that does control Massachusetts federal litigation.

Mandated reporter immunity (INP-01): repeated targeted searches of mass and massappct for a Massachusetts appellate decision construing the civil immunity clause of G. L. c. 119, section 51A returned nothing on point. Watterson v. Page (1st Cir.) construes a parallel state reporting-statute immunity and absolute witness immunity and is offered in its place; Kyle K. states the reporting duty itself.

Protective order without removal (ACT-05): no Massachusetts appellate decision was located treating a G. L. c. 209A abuse prevention order as a child protective alternative to removal. B.K. v. DCF (violation of a Probate and Family Court no-contact order supporting a neglect finding) and Adoption of Zander (judicial order barring a biological parent's contact) are the closest available Massachusetts authority.

PMC-01 through PMC-06 are federal oversight constructs (CFSR, HHS OIG and Single Audit Act reviews, CAPTA citizen review panels, the Protect Our Kids Act commission, FOIA). No Massachusetts or First Circuit decision construing any of those programs was located. The cases mapped to those nodes are the nearest Massachusetts authority on the underlying mechanics - the reasonable-efforts judicial determination that drives Title IV-E and CFSR measurement (Ilona), impoundment and public access to child welfare records (Adele), the public records law's disclosure presumption and custodian's burden (Mack, PETA), citizen volunteer participation through CASAs (Georgia), and accountability for harm to a child in state care (Sheila S., Beth). They should be read as analogues, not as authority on the federal programs themselves. PMC-02, PMC-03, PMC-04 and PMC-06 carry only two cases each for this reason.

Troxel v. Granville was retrieved and read but excluded: the controlling opinion is a four-Justice plurality, not a majority, so no quote from it satisfies the majority-opinion rule. Stanley v. Illinois is used instead for the parental-liberty and fitness-hearing baseline.

Two distinct SJC cases are captioned 'Custody of a Minor' in this brief: 375 Mass. 733 (1978), the leukemia chemotherapy case, and 383 Mass. 595 (1981), the unfitness/child's-wishes case. They are different cases with different cluster ids (2028378 and 2230315) and must not be merged.

Practice warning on standards of proof: Care & Protection of Robert fixes a fair preponderance standard at the seventy-two hour hearing under G. L. c. 119, section 24, while Care & Protection of Stephen, Care & Protection of Erin and Santosky require clear and convincing evidence at the merits trial, at review and redetermination, and at termination. Conflating the two is the most common error in this area. Separately, the administrative 'supported' finding under section 51B is reviewed only for substantial evidence supporting 'reasonable cause to believe' (Lindsay, Kyle K.) - a far lower bar than anything used in court.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the MA node files are keyword-matched Justia listings carrying synthetic citations (e.g. 'Massachusetts Court Of Appeals Case 22-p-35 (2023)'). Of those candidate titles, only Kyle K. v. Department of Children and Families was retrieved, read, and found on point; it is retained here with a corrected slip citation. The remainder (In re Grand Jury Investigation, Rhea R. v. DCF, In re Adoption of Patty, and the other keyword hits) were not verified as on point and are not carried forward.
Lassiter's date_decided is given as CourtListener records it (1981-08-28, the rehearing-denied date on the cluster). The opinion itself issued June 1, 1981; cite-check before filing.

Massachusetts has no central-registry statute of the kind found in many states; the analogous deprivation is DCF's registry of alleged perpetrators, and the concurrence in Kyle K. flags (without deciding) that a higher evidentiary showing may be constitutionally required to place a person on that registry than to support an allegation for service-provision purposes. That distinction is currently unresolved in Massachusetts law and is a live issue at DEC-03.

Missing (for a later pass): Adoption of Luc, 484 Mass. 139 (2020) — the SJC decision that actually governs when hearsay in a social worker's affidavit or report is admissible; Care and Protection of Doretta's holding (the brief's own DEC-04/ACT-03/INP-12 anchor) is expressly framed as applying Luc, so citing Doretta without Luc cites the application without the rule. Cite verified inside the retrieved Kyle K. opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Covell v. Department of Social Services, 439 Mass. 766 (2003) — the leading SJC authority on due process in DSS/DCF fair hearings and on substantial-evidence review of a 'supported' finding; Lindsay, Kyle K. and B.K. all build on it. Its absence leaves DEC-01 and DEC-03 resting on the downstream cases. Cite verified inside the retrieved Kyle K. opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Care & Protection of M.C., 483 Mass. 444 (2019) — the SJC's immediately preceding decision on public and press access to impounded care and protection records, and the source of the good-cause framework Adele applies. Missing from FAIL-06, PMC-05 and INP-09. Cite verified inside the retrieved Adele opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Adoption of Gregory, 434 Mass. 117 (2001) — the leading Massachusetts authority on disability and the department's obligation to accommodate a disabled parent in its reunification efforts; this is the genuine FAIL-05 discrimination authority the brief lacks (Magazu covers only religion). Cite verified inside the retrieved Adoption of Ilona opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Bezio v. Patenaude, 381 Mass. 563 (1980) — the foundational Massachusetts holding that a parent's status or lifestyle cannot support a custody deprivation absent a demonstrated nexus to harm to the child; the natural companion to Virgil at DEC-01/DEC-03 and the closest Massachusetts anti-discrimination holding for FAIL-05. Cite verified inside the retrieved Custody of a Minor, 383 Mass. 595, opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Care & Protection of Georgette, 439 Mass. 28 (2003) — the SJC decision of that name, distinct from the Appeals Court decision at 54 Mass. App. Ct. 778 that the brief carries; it governs the weight given to a child's wishes and the child's role as an interested party in care and protection proceedings. Its omission also creates a live citation-confusion trap alongside the Appeals Court case. Cite verified inside the retrieved Sophie and Uday opinions.

Missing (for a later pass): Care & Protection of Perry, 438 Mass. 1014 (2003) — the rescript that states the substantive standard applied at the seventy-two hour hearing (serious abuse or neglect, or immediate danger of it, plus necessity of immediate removal); Doretta quotes it as the operative test, so INP-12 and DEC-04 should carry it alongside Robert. Cite verified inside the retrieved Doretta opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Adoption of Mary, 414 Mass. 705 (1993) — the SJC authority repeatedly relied on for waiver of unpreserved claims and for child-specific findings in c. 119 and c. 210 proceedings; it is cited by both Georgette and Willow and belongs at FAIL-01.
